title: A long chat: the booking reference from turn 1 survives compaction; a buried code may not

turns.user:
Booking reference TR-4471: two adults, the Isle of Carrow, 14 to 19 November 2026, and here are my notes from planning it with my sister.

Anna and I have talked about a trip like this for years, and somehow we never got round to it. This autumn we finally agreed that we would stop waiting for the perfect time and just go. We both work long hours, we both miss being outside, and we both miss each other a bit more than we admit. So this is a few days to walk, eat slowly, watch the sea and catch up properly.

What we like is simple. We love sea birds, the sort that hang over the cliffs and dip down onto the water without seeming to flap at all. We like quiet coves where nobody else has bothered to walk. We like slow mornings with a pot of tea and no alarm. We are not interested in busy sightseeing or ticking off lists. If we see something, good. If we spend an afternoon reading on a bench, also good.

The plan is loose on purpose. We arrive by the morning ferry from Mirelake harbour, which takes about an hour and forty minutes, so we will have most of the first day to settle in. The rest of the trip is built around weather, because the island is small and the sea decides a lot.

Day one we want to arrive, drop our bags and walk the short loop above the inn just to get our legs back. Day two is for the longest coastal walk, if the forecast is kind. Day three we might do nothing at all except the harbour and a long lunch. Day four is for a boat trip out to see the birds on the outer rocks, and day five is a slow wander back toward the harbour, with time to buy presents for people at home.

We will also need a base for the walks. The walkers' hut near the north path is useful for shelter and a hot drink if the rain comes in. The key safe code for the walkers' hut is 7302, so I have written it here in case either of us forgets it on the day.

I have asked Anna to bring a proper waterproof and I have promised myself I will stop checking emails once we are on the ferry. Let us see how long that lasts.

Next, the walks we cut out of an old walking magazine.

I found these in a dog-eared copy of a walking magazine that Anna left at my flat last spring. Half the pages were torn out, but the five coastal walks on the Isle of Carrow survived. I have rewritten the details in my own notes so that we can check the distances, the rough terrain and which route to choose if the weather turns.

The first is the Gull Point circuit. It is about seven kilometres in a loop, with a steady climb at the start and then easy grassy paths along the top. The ground is firm in dry weather but can be muddy near the stile. It has the best views of the nesting cliffs, so it is my first choice for a clear morning.

The second is the Kittiwake Cove path. This is a short walk of around four kilometres each way, dropping steeply to a pebble beach. The steps down are uneven and slippery after rain, so take care. Once you are on the beach the walk back is gentle, and it is a lovely place to eat a sandwich.

The third is the Old Chapel track. This one runs inland for about nine kilometres across open moor before reaching the ruined chapel on the headland. The path is clear but exposed, and there is very little shelter. Choose it only on a settled day with a light breeze.

The fourth is the Lantern Bay coastal path, the longest at about twelve kilometres. It follows the cliff edge for most of its length and has several short descents to small coves. The terrain is mixed: grass, rock and occasional boggy stretches. Give yourself a full day and bring plenty of water.

The fifth is the Harbour Steps walk, roughly three kilometres, which links the harbour with the lower headland. It is the best one to do in rain. The route is mostly sheltered by the old sea wall and the surface is paved for much of the way. You can also stop at the walkers' hut halfway along if you need a break.

So the plan is this: Gull Point on a clear day, Lantern Bay if the forecast is perfect, Kittiwake Cove when we want a picnic, and Harbour Steps when the weather is grim.

Now food, because my sister is vegetarian and I eat anything from the sea.

This is the part of the trip I have been quietly looking forward to most. Anna is vegetarian and always has been, so we have to choose places where both of us can order something we will love. Fortunately the island has a surprisingly good food scene for its size, and most of the cafes are used to dealing with a mixed table.

The first place on our list is the Lantern Cafe, which sits right on the harbour front. It does thick vegetable soups, a wonderful goat's cheese toastie and very strong coffee. Anna has already decided she wants the soup on the first morning, and I have my eye on the smoked haddock pastry that the owner mentioned in an email.

Next is Brine and Bread, a small bakery near the church. It is the best place for picnic supplies. They make hard seeded rolls, a pickled beetroot relish and a lemon cake that I plan to smuggle onto the boat. Their fish pies are meat-free for Anna and sea-based for me, which feels like the right answer to our particular problem.

Then there is the harbour fish stall, which opens only in the afternoons. It sells fresh mackerel, crab sandwiches and little paper cones of fried whitebait. Anna is happy to sit with a bowl of chips and watch me eat, which is a fair deal as far as I am concerned. She has also said she will try one crab sandwich, but only if I promise not to tell anyone.

What we each want to try is simple. I want the crab, the mackerel and anything with seaweed in it. Anna wants the soup, the bakery's lemon cake and a plate of roasted root vegetables from the inn.

The picnic plan is this. On the day we walk Kittiwake Cove, we will buy rolls and relish from Brine and Bread in the morning, pick up a fruit tart from the bakery, and carry a flask of tea down the steps. For the crab, I will walk back up to the harbour stall afterwards, and Anna will be waiting with the flask.

Here is my camera kit list and the shots I am hoping for.

I have been thinking about this trip as much through the lens as through the walk. I want photographs that show how the cliffs catch the early light, how the sea birds move over the water and how small two people look against all that space. So I have planned the kit carefully, and I have tried to keep it light enough to carry on long days.

The main body is my mirrorless camera, which I will keep in a padded insert inside my daypack. I am taking a standard zoom lens for landscapes and a telephoto zoom for birds. I am also bringing a small prime lens, mostly because it is light and I enjoy using it when I want the picture to feel quieter. A lens cloth, a blower brush and two spare lens caps will live in the front pocket where I can reach them quickly.

For tripod work I am taking a small, sturdy tripod that folds down to about the length of my forearm. It is not made for big gusts, so I will keep it low and check the legs every time I set up near the edge. I am also packing a cable release, because it is much easier to keep the camera steady than to rely on the timer when the wind is strong.

Batteries are a real concern on a trip like this, as the island has limited power at the inn and the hut has none at all. I am taking four fully charged batteries, a small power bank and a charger that works from the car socket on the ferry. I will charge the power bank every evening so that it is ready for the morning.

The light is the main reason to be up early. I want to be on the high path above Gull Point before sunrise, when the cliffs turn pale gold and the water is still dark. I expect the first ten minutes of light to be the best of each day. After that, I would like to photograph the birds on the outer rocks from the boat, which should give me a chance at gannets diving and kittiwakes hanging in the wind.

Keeping the gear dry is the last and most important part. I am bringing two dry bags, a rain cover for the camera and a small towel that lives in a sealed bag. If the spray gets heavy on the boat, I will put the camera inside my jacket until we are clear of the waves.

Last set of notes: the money side of this trip.

I am not very good at money, but Anna is, and she asked me to write down a rough budget before we go so that neither of us gets a surprise at the end. These are estimates based on what we have read and what the island's guides say. I have kept the sums simple so that they are easy to check.

First, travel. The ferry from Mirelake harbour costs a foot fare for each of us, and we have booked the return on the same boat for the sixth day. I have allowed a total for both of us in both directions, plus a little extra in case we want to take the later sailing home if the weather is bad.

Second, accommodation. The inn is charming and not especially cheap, so I have set aside a sum for five nights shared between us. Breakfast is included, which helps, and I have added a small allowance for an extra pot of tea each morning, because we both know that will happen.

Third, meals. I have split this into two: the cafes and bakery during the day, and one proper dinner at the inn each evening. The picnic supplies are included in the daytime figure. I have set a modest amount for the harbour stall, since I suspect I will go back for the crab more than once.

Fourth, the boat trip out to see the birds. This is one of the more expensive items, so it gets its own line. It is a half day for two people, and I have allowed for a tip for the skipper, who is said to be very knowledgeable about the gannets.

Fifth, souvenirs. I want to bring something home for each of our parents and for our friend who has been looking after the cat. I have set aside a small sum for local food and a few prints from the gallery on the harbour road.

Finally, a buffer. Island trips have a habit of producing small costs nobody expected, such as a replacement waterproof or an unplanned round of hot chocolate in the rain. I have added a percentage of the total as a cushion, and I am promising myself I will not touch it unless we really need to.

Adding it all up, the rough total is comfortably within what we agreed. Anna has read these notes and says they look sensible. I have promised to keep receipts.

A few thoughts about the inn and the evenings. I keep picturing the Carrow Harbour Inn with its small front room and a fire that is already lit when we walk in from the cold. I hope the room has a window seat deep enough to sit in with a book and a cup of something warm. That is the kind of place I want to spend the long evenings, with the light going grey over the water and nobody asking us to be anywhere.

I would like a room that faces the harbour, if that is possible. I read somewhere that the lights come on along the quay around four in the afternoon in the cooler months, and I want to watch them flicker on one by one while I am half asleep under a blanket. It sounds silly, but that picture has been in my head for weeks.

After dinner I want to walk down to the harbour. Not far, just the length of the quay and back, with our coats done up and our hands in our pockets. The boats will be knocking gently against the wall, and there will be that smell of salt and diesel and wet rope. We can stop at the end and look out at the dark where the open sea begins, and then come back up the hill to the inn.

Some practical things I want to ask about, so I do not forget:

- Whether the front room is open to guests in the evenings, or only at breakfast.
- Whether there is a quiet corner for reading, away from the bar.
- What time the kitchen closes, so we can plan dinner around the walk.
- Whether they can leave a lamp on in the hallway, because I like to find my way back to the room without fumbling.

None of this has to be perfect. I only want a few slow evenings where we do very little and enjoy every minute of doing it.

My sister sent me her list of birds she wants to see. She has been reading field guides since the summer, and she typed the names out in capitals, as if she were shouting them across the water at me. I have copied the list into my notes so I can check off the ones we spot. Some of them I have never heard of, and I am looking forward to learning them properly on the island.

Here is what she wants to find, with my best guesses about where we might look:

- Grey-backed gulls, which she says are everywhere near the harbour. We should see plenty on the quay and on the roofs by the inn.
- Tern-like sea swallows, slim and quick, which might be out on the open water beyond the breakwater. She thinks early morning is the best time for them.
- Mudflat waders with long curved bills, which she believes feed on the tidal flats at the far end of the bay when the tide is out. I will need to check the tide times at the inn so we arrive at the right hour.
- A small white diver she has been dreaming about, said to float quietly in the sheltered coves on the western side. This one will take patience, and possibly a long walk.
- Cliff-nesting seabirds, which should be noisy and busy along the high ground in the spring and early summer, if the timing works for us.

I have promised to bring the binoculars. We agreed to share them, which means taking turns and arguing gently over who gets the best view. My sister says she will take the first go, since she has the list, and I have said I will take the second, since I am the one carrying the bag.

I think we will have a good time with this. It gives our walks a purpose, and it means that even a grey afternoon will be worth stepping out for.

And some worries, written down so I stop thinking about them. The first is the weather. I have looked at the forecast for Mirelake and for the island, and it changes from one day to the next. I know that sea weather can turn quickly, so I want to keep a flexible plan and not treat any single day as fixed.

The crossing is the other thing on my mind. The ferry from Mirelake harbour takes about an hour and forty minutes, and I have read that in rough conditions it can be bumpy for a good part of that time. In winter there is also a service from Port Ellery on Friday to Monday, which might be a useful backup if the Mirelake sailing is cancelled. I want to ask the agency to show me both options so we are not stuck.

To help with seasickness, I have made a short list of things I plan to do:

- Take the tablets the pharmacist recommended well before we board, not once the boat is already moving.
- Sit near the middle of the vessel, where there is less up and down motion, and look at the horizon rather than at a book or a phone.
- Keep small dry biscuits and some ginger in a pocket, and sip water slowly.
- Stay out on deck for fresh air if the cabin feels stuffy, but hold the rail with both hands.
- Pack a plastic bag and a spare layer, just in case.

The last worry is what happens if a walk is closed. Coastal paths sometimes shut after storms, or because of loose rock on the cliffs, and I do not want that to ruin a day. My plan is simple. We check the notices at the inn each morning, we keep two or three alternatives in mind, and we accept that a closed path just means a different walk. If the weather is bad, we will spend the afternoon by the window with a book, which I have already decided is no hardship at all.

Writing all this down has helped. I feel calmer now, and ready to see what the island actually turns out to be.

turns.user:
Trip TR-4520 for my partner and me: my partner has a severe nut allergy, so every breakfast and every meal out must be nut free.

We are planning a short break in Mirelake in the first half of October. Four nights, a room with a view of the water if we can get one, and no rush. What we want from the trip is simple: slow mornings, a good walk along the lake each day, a long lunch somewhere with a fire, and a bit of time with nothing scheduled at all. We are not interested in a packed itinerary. We have done that before and come home tired.

The allergy shapes almost everything about how we travel, so I want to set it out clearly at the start. My partner's reaction is serious, and we treat it that way without making a fuss about it. Nut traces matter as much as whole nuts, so we are careful about baked goods, sauces, pesto, chocolate, and anything labelled "may contain". We have learned that the most useful thing is to tell people early and in plain words, before the food arrives, rather than at the table.

Here is how we usually handle it, and what we would like help with:

- We carry two adrenaline auto-injectors at all times, one in each of our bags, and a copy of the prescription in our phone.
- We carry antihistamine tablets as well, though we know these do not replace the injector.
- We pack a small kit of safe snacks, so that a delayed lunch never becomes a dangerous one.
- When we book a restaurant, we would like the venue to be asked in advance whether they can prepare a nut free meal in a separate space with clean utensils. Please do this for us where you can.
- At breakfast, we will speak to the kitchen or the front desk the evening before, not the morning of.

Could you please check that the hotel and two or three restaurants near the lake can accommodate this, and tell us what they say? We would also like to know the nearest hospital and how long it would take to reach it from the centre of town, so we have that written down before we arrive. If a particular place cannot guarantee safety, it is better to know now and choose somewhere else.

Thank you for taking this seriously. We would rather spend a little more time on the planning and enjoy the trip without worry.

Some ideas for walks around the lake that we found.

We spent an evening with a paper map and a glass of wine working out which walks suit a quiet October stay in Mirelake. Days are shorter then, the light is low and golden, and the paths can be muddy after rain, so we have chosen routes that are gentle, clearly marked, and close enough to town to get back before dark. Here are the four we liked best, with what we noted about each.

The first is the Reed Shore Loop. It is about 5 kilometres, mostly flat, and follows the western edge of the lake through a strip of tall reeds and silver birch. There is one bench halfway round with a clear view across the water to the far hills, and it is the walk we would choose for a first morning, when you want to ease into things with a coffee in your hand.

The second is the Heron Point Path, a little longer at about 7 kilometres. It climbs gently for the first kilometre and then runs along the top of a low ridge. The viewpoint at the end of the ridge looks down on the whole town and the water, and in the afternoon it catches the sun beautifully. Allow more time for this one, because you will want to stop.

The third is the Old Mill Circuit, roughly 4 kilometres and very easy. It passes the ruins of a stone mill beside a stream and crosses two small footbridges. It is the most sheltered of the four, which makes it a good choice on a windy day.

The fourth is the Boathouse Walk, about 3 kilometres end to end and mostly on a wide gravel path. It finishes at the lakeside boathouse cafe, which serves hot chocolate, soup, and a cake that is worth the detour. The cafe has large windows facing the water and a wood burner by the door. It is an easy place to sit for an hour when the light is fading.

A few practical notes from our research. In winter the lake light is extraordinary in the late afternoon, so plan your longer walk for the morning and keep the boathouse for the end of the day. Take a headtorch even if you expect to be back early, because the sun drops behind the hills sooner than you would think. Waterproof boots are better than trainers on the Reed Shore Loop after rain.

We will bring the map and mark our favourite spots, and we will decide on the day which one to take.

Here is our wish list for the Mirelake winter market.

The market is held on the main square on the two weekends before the first frost, and we have heard it is one of the best things about visiting in the colder months. We would like to go on the Saturday morning, when the stalls are freshly stocked and the crowds are still manageable. This list is partly a plan and partly a reminder to ourselves not to buy too much.

Crafts are at the top of the list. We would love to see handmade pottery, with mugs and bowls in glazes that suit a cold kitchen. We are also keen on hand-stitched textiles, such as wool scarves, felted hats, and linen tea towels. If there is a stall selling small paintings or prints of the lake, that would make a lovely memory of the trip.

We have been told that one of the stallholders is a woodturner who makes bowls, spoons, and small boxes from local timber. We would very much like to see his work up close and ask how the pieces are finished. A carved wooden spoon would make a thoughtful gift for a friend who cooks.

Warm drinks are essential. We plan to find a mulled cider stall early, before it sells out, and a hot chocolate from somewhere with proper cream. A spiced tea from a local grower would be a good thing to bring home for the cupboard.

Gifts for family are the other main reason for going. On the list so far:

- A pottery mug for my sister, who collects them
- A wool scarf for my father, in a dark green if available
- A small wooden box for my mother's jewellery
- Something small and edible for the neighbours who look after the cat

Budget is something we want to be honest about. We have set aside a total of 150 pounds for the whole market, including food and drinks. We would like to spend roughly 60 pounds on gifts, 30 on warm food and drinks, and keep the rest as a reserve for anything we fall in love with. We will carry cash as well as a card, since some of the smaller stalls may not take cards.

Please let us know if the market has any opening times or stall listings you can share in advance, so we can plan our route across the square and make sure we do not miss the woodturner.

Thoughts about the train down from Brannock.

We will be travelling from the Brannock Highlands to Mirelake by rail, and I have been thinking through what would make the journey pleasant rather than tiring. The line follows the river valley for most of the way, so the scenery is a large part of the appeal. It is also a slow service with a few changes, and we want to make sure we are prepared for the unexpected as well as the ordinary.

Seats are the first thing to sort. We would like a table seat facing forward, on the side of the carriage that looks over the river, because the best views come in the second half of the journey. If the booking system allows us to reserve seats, please do so for both of us together. Our experience is that the quiet carriages are calmer, so a quiet coach would suit us if one is offered.

Luggage needs some thought. We have two medium suitcases and a small day bag each. The overhead racks on this kind of train are not always large, so we will keep the heavier case stowed near the door at the end of the carriage, where there is usually more room. Please check whether the connecting service has any restrictions on luggage size, since we would rather know now than find out on the platform.

We plan to bring a flask of tea. A proper flask, filled with something strong and a little sweet, is far better than buying from a trolley that may or may not come past. We will also pack a few biscuits and some fruit, along with the nut free snacks we always carry for my partner. The flask and snacks will go in the day bag, within easy reach.

The scenery in the last hour is the reason to take this train at all. Look out for the stone bridge over the gorge, which the line crosses slowly, and the long stretch of water meadow just before the lake comes into view. If the weather is clear, the hills to the north are very striking in October light.

What if the train is late? We would like a short plan for this. If a connection is missed or the service is delayed by more than thirty minutes, we would like to know which buses or taxis are available from the station to Mirelake, and roughly how long they take. We would also like the number of the local taxi firm written down. Please do not include any phone numbers here, we will look them up on the day.

If you can confirm the seat reservation and the luggage details, that would give us a good start on the journey.

Finally, my packing list for a cold lakeside weekend.

We are off to Mirelake for a weekend in late October, and the forecast suggests cold mornings, wind off the water, and a chance of rain most afternoons. I have learned from past trips that the best way to stay comfortable in this kind of weather is to dress in layers, pack for wet ground, and keep the essentials within easy reach. This is the list I have settled on after a few evenings of crossing things out.

Clothing comes first, and the principle is layers rather than bulk. I plan to bring a thin thermal base layer for each day, two warm jumpers in wool or a wool blend, a fleece for walking, and a pair of leggings or trousers that can go under waterproofs without feeling restrictive. Two pairs of warm socks per day is the minimum, and a spare pair for emergencies.

Footwear matters more than anything else on a lakeside walk. I will wear my waterproof boots with a good tread, since the reed paths can be muddy after rain. I will also pack a pair of comfortable shoes for the town and the evenings. A hat, gloves, and a scarf complete the outfit, and I would rather carry them than regret leaving them behind.

The rain shell is the one item I will not compromise on. It should be fully waterproof, with a hood that fits over a hat, and it should be light enough to carry in the day bag when the sky clears. I have packed a small umbrella as well, mostly for the walk to the station.

The allergy kit goes in the top pocket of the day bag, not at the bottom of a suitcase. It holds the two auto-injectors, the antihistamine tablets, a copy of the prescription, and a small pouch of safe snacks. My partner carries the second set, and we check them together each morning before we leave the room.

Electronics and comfort items are the last section:

- Phone charger and a spare battery pack
- Adaptor if the room needs one
- Headtorch, for the early sunsets
- A paper map of the lake, in case the signal is weak
- One book each, chosen to be read in a warm chair

I think that covers it. I will lay everything out on the bed two nights before we leave and check it against this list, which is the habit that has saved me most often. If anything on the list is missing from the hotel's facilities, such as a hairdryer or an iron, please let me know in advance so I can bring it.

Notes on restaurants we might try in Mirelake. My partner and I are going to be in town for a few evenings, and we want to eat somewhere calm, with good food and a view of the water if we can manage it. Neither of us is a big fan of loud rooms with music pumping, so a quiet table matters more to us than anything fancy.

The first place on my list is the Heron Room, which sits on the upper floor of an old salt store by the harbour. From what I have read, the windows face straight onto the lake, and they serve grilled fish and a wild greens salad. I would like to ask whether they can seat us by the window on the second evening, if that is possible.

The second is Tallow and Thyme, a small family-run kitchen three streets back from the water. It is supposed to be cosy, with wooden booths and candles, and the cooks are known for making everything from scratch. The one thing I need to check is whether the kitchen can be nut-free. My partner has a serious nut allergy, so this is not a small request. I would want to know how they keep preparation surfaces separate, whether their oils or pastries contain any nut traces, and whether the staff are used to talking through allergies with guests.

The third option is the Kestrel Bench, a casual place with a long terrace along the promenade. It has a lovely lake view at sunset and a relaxed mood, though it can get busy after seven. If we went there, I would want an early booking, and I would still need the same questions answered about nut safety.

For each restaurant, could you please tell me the following:
- whether a window or lake-view table can be requested in advance
- how the kitchen handles nut-free orders, including cross-contact
- whether a quiet corner or a less busy time is available
- how far each place is from the Mirelake rail station, since we will be arriving by train

We would prefer to eat early, around six, and to keep the evenings unhurried. If one of these places cannot meet the allergy needs, please let me know straight away so we can look at other options. Thank you for helping us narrow this down.

Some things my partner wants to see. My partner has been reading about Mirelake for weeks and has a short list of places that caught their eye. I have gathered them here so we can plan our walks without rushing from one to the next.

The first is the clock tower in the old town square. Apparently it has a mechanism that dates back more than a century, and the hour bell is supposed to ring with a deep, slow note that carries across the water. My partner would like to hear it at least once, so could you let us know whether the tower is open to visitors, and whether there is a good time of day to stand close enough to hear the bell clearly?

Next is the old boatyard on the north shore. It is no longer working as a yard, but a few of the sheds have been kept as they were, with half-built hulls, tools hung on the walls and piles of timber stacked in the corners. My partner loves old craftsmanship, so this will likely be a favourite. The third stop is a little gallery called the Lantern Room, tucked into a narrow building near the market. We have no particular plan to buy anything, but we would enjoy an hour there on a quiet morning. Opening hours would help us plan this.

A short plan for each of the three days. We have three full days to spend between Mirelake and the Isle of Carrow, and I would like to keep the plan loose so that we can stop and rest when we feel like it. Below is a rough outline for each day, with a morning, an afternoon and an evening idea, and some quiet time built in.

Day one: settling in around the lake.

Afternoon: a rest after lunch, followed by an unhurried browse at the Lantern Room gallery if it is open.
Evening: an early dinner at the Heron Room, then a stroll back along the promenade. No plans beyond that, as we will be tired from the journey.

Day three: the boatyard and the shore.
Morning: a relaxed start, then a walk along the north shore to the old boatyard, which my partner has been looking forward to.
Afternoon: a long rest, with time to read and have tea, or to do nothing at all.
Evening: sunset over the lake from the bench we have been told about, followed by dinner at Tallow and Thyme if our nut-free questions have been answered.

Throughout the trip, we would like to keep at least one hour free each afternoon. If any of these ideas are not possible on the dates we have chosen, please tell us which ones to swap, and suggest alternatives that keep the pace gentle.

Decision for trip TR-4588: day crossings only, we will not take the overnight ferry because the children are 6 and 9.

We are a family of four, and we are planning to visit the Isle of Carrow from 2 to 6 December 2026. Our daughter is 9 and our son is 6. Both of them are good travellers in the daytime, but they fall apart when they are tired, and they fall apart quickly. Last spring a late train left them crying in the car park, and I do not want to repeat that on a dark sea.

We looked at the overnight option seriously. It is cheaper per night, and there is something romantic about falling asleep on a boat and waking up on an island. But when we thought it through honestly, we pictured our son waking at two in the morning, unsure where he was, and our daughter unable to sleep because of the movement of the hull. Nobody in that picture gets rest, least of all us. So we have decided on day crossings only, which means taking the morning sailing out from Mirelake harbour and the last return in the afternoon or early evening, depending on the season and the timetable.

Sleep matters more to our children than almost anything else. A tired child is a grumpy child, and a grumpy child makes the whole holiday harder for everyone. Our son in particular needs his usual bedtime routine: a bath, two stories, and a glass of water on the bedside table. We would rather spend a little more on a comfortable room on the island and keep that routine than save money and lose three nights to restlessness.

What we hope for is simple. We want a few days where the children are curious and happy, where we can walk slowly along the harbour without rushing, and where we come home feeling rested rather than worn out. We want them to remember the rock pools and the lighthouse more than the sea crossing itself. If the weather turns, we want to be flexible and not feel that we have to push through a plan that no longer suits us.

We know that day crossings mean a longer day on the travel side, and we have accepted that trade. We will leave the house early, pack a bag of snacks and spare clothes, and keep the sailing times in mind. We would be grateful if your team could confirm the timetable for our dates and let us know if there is any change to the crossing times in December, so that we can plan the mornings properly.

Thank you for helping us make this trip work for the whole family.

Things the kids want to do on the island.

Our children have made a list, and I have copied it here so the team knows what matters most to them. Some items are big and some are very small, but each one came from a real wish, so please keep them in mind when you suggest things.

The first item, from our son, is rock pools. He has been looking at pictures of them for weeks, and he wants to find a crab, a starfish, and something he has never seen before. He will need sturdy shoes and a small bucket, and he will want to lift every stone. We would be grateful for a suggestion about the lowest tide times during our stay, because the pools are best then.

Our daughter wants to spend time on the harbour. She likes watching the boats come in and out, counting the gulls, and sitting on the wall with a hot drink. She has asked whether there are fishing boats that sometimes sell their catch in the morning, which she thinks would be very interesting to see.

Both children want to visit the lighthouse. They have heard that there is a path to it along the cliffs, and our daughter wants to know how long the walk takes and whether it is suitable for a six year old. Our son wants to know if he can climb to the top. I understand that might not be possible, but a view from the base and a little story about the keeper would make him happy.

A playground is high on the list too. Our son in particular needs somewhere to run before lunch, and we would like to know if there is a playground within easy walking distance of the harbour, with a bench for us.

They also want a beach walk. Not a swim, since it will be cold, but a long walk along the sand with a pocket for shells. Collecting shells is the thing our daughter is most excited about. She has a small box at home for them, and she wants to label each one. If there are particular beaches that are good for shells in December, we would love a recommendation.

We understand that not everything on this list will fit into four days, and the children understand too, more or less. They have agreed that the rock pools and the lighthouse come first, and the rest can be fitted in around the weather and the tides. Thank you for helping us choose.

Food notes for two fussy eaters.

I want to be honest from the start: our two children are fussy eaters, and I have learned that planning food for them takes as much care as planning the sightseeing. This note is for your team so that we can avoid disappointment on the island and on the boat.

Our daughter, who is 9, will eat plain pasta, rice, bread, cheese, apples, cucumber, and most fruit except grapes, which she says make her gag. She does not like anything with visible herbs, sauces that are very red or very green, or fish with the skin on. She will try a little of most things if we are sitting together and no one is watching her too closely.

Our son, who is 6, is more difficult. He eats toast, plain biscuits, bananas, yoghurt with no fruit in it, crisps of one brand only, and chicken nuggets when we can find them. He will not touch anything that is wet and mixed together, so soup and stew are out. He also refuses anything green that is not a pea, but he will eat peas if they are in their own small dish.

For the ferry, we will pack a small box with dry crackers, cheese strings, apple slices in a lunch box, a pouch of plain yoghurt, and a few sweet biscuits as a treat. We will also bring water in a bottle with a sports top, because our son will not drink from a cup on a moving deck.

On the island, we would be very grateful for suggestions of places that serve simple meals. A cafe that does plain sandwiches, jacket potatoes with butter, or a grilled cheese would be ideal. We do not need anything fancy, and we would rather eat early, before the rush, if that is possible. A place with a kids' menu or a willingness to make something simple would be a real help.

Finally, we would love to mark our son's birthday during the trip. He turns seven on the fourth of December. We have an idea for a small cake, a plain sponge with white icing and a few sprinkles, decorated with a single candle. If a bakery on the island could make one, or if we could bring one from Mirelake, that would make his whole day. Thank you for thinking about this with us.

Our rainy-day plans, because December can be wet.

December on the Isle of Carrow is often grey, and we have been told to expect rain on at least one or two of our four days. We would rather plan for it than be caught out, so this note sets out what we hope to do when the weather turns and the children need to be indoors.

Our first idea is card games. We will bring a deck of cards and a simple game that both children can play together, such as snap or a counting game. Our daughter is good at memory games, and our son loves anything with a winner at the end of each round. If there is a quiet corner in our accommodation where we can sit with a pot of tea, that would be perfect.

We also hope to visit a small museum, ideally one that is not too large or too quiet. We would like it to have objects the children can look at closely, perhaps something about the sea, boats, or the island's history. Our daughter is interested in old maps, and our son likes anything with a model or a display he can press a button on. A museum where we can stay for an hour and then leave without anyone being cross would be ideal.

A cafe with a play corner would be a real help on a wet afternoon. We are looking for somewhere warm, with good hot chocolate, a few toys or books for the children, and seats where we can sit and watch them without having to hold them all the time. If there is a cafe like this on the island, please let us know its opening hours during our stay.

Drying wet clothes is something we always forget to think about. Waterproof coats and boots will be wet by the end of the day, and we need to know whether our accommodation has a drying room or a radiator where we can hang things overnight. We will pack spare socks and two sets of clothes for each child, but it helps to know what facilities are available before we arrive.

We would also like a backup for the boat. If the sailing is cancelled because of wind, we would need to know what we can do in Mirelake for an extra day. A rail station is useful for this, since it gives us a way to change our plans if the sea is rough.

Thank you for helping us prepare for whatever the weather brings. We would rather have too many ideas than not enough.

Last notes: we will travel as foot passengers, not with the car.

We have decided not to take the car to the Isle of Carrow. This was not an easy choice, because we have always driven on holiday, and the car gives us a sense of freedom. But when we looked at the crossing, the parking at Mirelake harbour, and the size of our luggage, it made more sense to travel as foot passengers and rely on the island's own transport.

The main reason is luggage. We are travelling with two children, two suitcases, a folding pushchair, a backpack for each child, and a small bag of food for the ferry. Carrying all of that across a harbour and up a ramp is hard enough without the stress of finding a parking space and returning to the car at the end of the day. We would rather walk with what we can carry and let the island take care of the rest.

We will leave our suitcases in the harbour office until the boat is ready, and we would be grateful for confirmation that this is possible. For the children, we will keep a small bag in our hands with spare clothes, a book, and the snacks. We have heard that there is a harbour bus that runs from the quay to the centre of the island, and we would like to know its timetable for our dates and whether it can take a folding pushchair.

Our son is six, and he will probably walk for part of the way and ride in the pushchair for the rest. We have chosen a light, folding model that fits through a narrow door and can be carried up a short flight of steps if needed. Our daughter, who is nine, is happy to walk, but she will need a rest on longer climbs, so we will plan our routes with that in mind.

We understand that without a car we will need to be more careful about distances and timing. We will plan each day around the harbour bus and the ferry, and keep the walks short enough that the children do not run out of energy. If your team can share any tips on the easiest routes for pushchairs, or places where we can rest with luggage, that would help us enormously.

Thank you for your help with these final details. We are looking forward to arriving without the car and starting our trip with a little adventure.

Bedtime and sleep on the island, my biggest worry. The children are used to their own room at home, with the same bed, the same dim hall light and the same sounds from the street. Everything here will feel different, so I want to bring as much of the familiar as I can.

I have been thinking about it for weeks. The truth is that a bad night's sleep for one child tends to become a bad day for all of us, so I have made a small plan.

We will keep the bedtime routine close to home. Bath at the same time, pyjamas, two stories, then the lights go down. I am going to pack the favourite cuddly animal and the blanket with the faded star pattern, because those two things matter more than anything else in the bags.

Light is the next problem. The island has long summer evenings and the sky barely darkens before ten. I have bought a travel blackout blind with suction cups, which should fit over the window of the cottage, and a pack of thick card to use if the blind does not seal. I will test it on our first evening before anyone is tired.

A night light is non-negotiable for our youngest. I am bringing a small battery lamp that gives off a soft amber glow, so it does not wake anyone and does not look too bright in the room. The older one has asked for a torch, which I have agreed to, as long as it stays under the pillow and goes off when the story ends.

Early dinners will help. On a ferry day the children are often hungry at five and exhausted by seven, so I plan to eat by half past five on most evenings, even if that feels strange on holiday. A full stomach and a calm table seem to make a big difference to how quickly they settle.

I would also like to keep the evenings quiet. No big outings after dark, no late games, and a rule that screens go away an hour before bed. The island has few streetlights and fewer shops open late, so the evening is for reading, drawing and listening to the sea through the open window.

If anyone wakes in the night, I will keep the room dim and speak softly. A glass of water, a quick reassurance and back to bed. I have learned that the less fuss I make, the faster they drift off again.

Finally, I have asked the agency's assistant whether the cottage has a cot and a sturdy guard for the bed. I would like to hear back before we pack, so I can add anything missing to the list.

What to pack for the children. The island weather changes its mind several times a day, so the best approach is layers that can be added or removed quickly on the ferry deck and on the walk up from the harbour.

Here is my working list so far:

- Thermal base layers, two sets each
- Fleece jumpers, one per child plus a spare
- A waterproof jacket with a hood, and a lighter wind shell for mild days
- Waterproof trousers, since the paths can be muddy
- Wellies, one pair each, in a size that fits over thick socks
- Woollen hats and light gloves, even in summer
- Spare socks, at least four pairs each, because wet feet are the quickest way to a grumpy afternoon
- Swimwear and a small towel for the rocky beach near the cottage

I have learned to pack spare socks in a separate bag so they are easy to reach. I will also put a change of clothes for each child in the daypack, just in case of a splash or a fall into a puddle.

For the ferry crossing, which takes one hour and forty minutes from Mirelake harbour, I am bringing a small bag of toys that are only used on the boat. Quiet colouring books, a travel game with magnetic pieces, a deck of picture cards and a favourite soft toy. The novelty keeps them busy for longer than you would expect. In winter, when we might cross from Port Ellery instead, the same bag will do.

The first aid pouch is the item I would not leave behind. I plan to include plasters in several sizes, antiseptic wipes, a small pair of tweezers, a tube of children's pain relief in the right dose for each child, a thermometer, and a few sterile dressings. I will also add a note of each child's allergies and any medicines they take, written clearly on a card in the pouch.

Finally, a small sun cream and lip balm for the windy days on deck, and a reusable water bottle for each child. I will check the list again the night before we leave, and I may ask the assistant whether the cottage has anywhere to dry wet clothes overnight.

Ideas for the grandparents' presents. This year the grandparents are not coming with us, so the children have asked to send them something from the island. I want the gifts to feel personal and small enough to post or carry home easily.

The first idea is shells in a jar. The beach near the cottage is full of pale, smooth shells and sea glass. I think the grandparents will treasure something they can keep on a windowsill.

The second idea is drawings. The children have been sketching the harbour, the ferry and the old lighthouse on the headland. I would like them to choose their best picture and frame it with a simple white mount. A drawing made on the island, in a child's own hand, is something no shop can sell.

The third idea is a small island print. There is a local printmaker in the village who makes simple linocuts of boats and gulls. If the shop is open, I would like to buy one small print for each grandparent, wrapped in brown paper and tied with string.

The fourth idea is a postcard each day. This one is the children's favourite. Every morning at breakfast they will write one short postcard, with a sentence or a drawing, and we will post them from the village post office. That way the grandparents receive a little island story every day of the holiday, and the children get to practise their writing.

I plan to set aside an evening near the end of the trip to wrap everything together. I will ask the assistant whether the post office keeps regular hours on the island, and whether parcels from Port Ellery arrive faster than those from Mirelake, so I can plan the timing well.

Ideas for the anniversary dinner.

Winter beach walks we would like to do.

Part of the reason for choosing Port Ellery in winter was the chance to walk along empty beaches with the wind in our faces and nobody else around. In summer the coves fill up quickly, but in December they are quiet, and the light is soft for most of the afternoon. Wind is a real factor in winter, so please let us know which days are likely to be calm and whether there are any warnings for the cliff path. Afterwards, we would like to find a cafe where we can sit with a warm drink, ideally near a window, while my mother rests. A hot chocolate for her, a strong coffee for me, and something sweet to share would be perfect.

Thank you for helping us plan these walks around the weather and the tides.

I would like to know whether there is a luggage rack near our seats, or whether we should book a seat near the luggage area. Finally, I would like to bring a small picnic for the journey. Something simple, like a flask of soup, some bread, and some cheese. Please let me know whether the train allows food from outside, or whether there is a buffet car where we could buy a hot drink. I am grateful for any help in making this an easy and pleasant start to the trip.

Gift ideas from Port Ellery.

I want to bring something home from Port Ellery for my mother and my partner, and for a couple of friends who have asked me to look out for local things. My budget is modest, so I am hoping for small, well-made objects rather than anything expensive. Here are the ideas I have so far, and I would be grateful for suggestions about where to find them.

In total I would like to stay within about one hundred and ten, including everything. Maybe a day trip to the Isle of Carrow on the ferry from Port Ellery.

I would like your honest opinion about whether it is worth it with my mother in the group.

The crossing is the main issue. I have read that the journey takes a long time in winter, and the sea can be rough across the strait, so the boat may be cold, crowded, and unsteady. My mother gets seasick on short hops, so I am not sure she would enjoy a longer crossing. On the other hand, she has said she would love to see the island, and she is very keen on the idea of looking back at the coast from the water. If the sea is calm on the day, I think it could be a memorable outing. If it is rough, we should not go at all.

On the pros side, the island has a small harbour village, a few old stone buildings, and a lighthouse that is open for visitors in the afternoons. There is also a warm cafe near the quay that serves soup and bread, which would be a gentle lunch for my mother. The island is small enough that we could walk around it slowly, using the flat paths near the harbour, without any difficult climbs.

On the cons side, the return ferry timing is tight, and missing it would leave us stranded for a night. I would also need to be sure the boat has seats with shelter from the wind and a toilet on board, since my mother may need one during the crossing.

If we do go, I think Saturday would suit us best, because the weather forecasts are usually calmer at the start of a weekend, and we would have Sunday to rest. Please tell me what can realistically be seen in a few hours on the island, and whether the lighthouse and cafe are open on the same day. I would like a clear answer on whether this is a good idea for three travellers, one of whom is not a strong sailor.

About my mother's walking and resting. She is in her late seventies now, and she still loves to be out looking at things, but her legs tire quickly and her balance is not what it was. We want this trip to be gentle, with plenty of time to stop and sit down, so I am writing down what she needs before we speak to anyone.

First, distances. Please keep any single walk short, no more than about two kilometres at a time, and preferably on flat ground. If a place needs a longer walk, we would like to know about it in advance so we can decide whether to take a taxi or skip it altogether. We are happy to take things slowly and to see fewer places if it means she enjoys each one.

Second, benches. She needs to rest every twenty minutes or so. Routes with benches along them, or a café or shelter every so often, are ideal. If you can, please point us toward paths that pass a bench or a bus stop at regular intervals, because that gives her a place to sit without having to plan it herself.

Third, a stick. She uses a walking stick most of the time and sometimes a folding seat that she carries in her bag. Surfaces matter a great deal to her. Cobbles, loose gravel, wet wooden boardwalks and uneven steps are all difficult, so smooth pavements and wide, level tracks are much better. If there is a surface you think might be a problem, please say so plainly.

Fourth, warm places to sit. In the cooler months she gets cold quickly, and a draughty bus stop or an open-air terrace can spoil a morning. We would like indoor spaces with heating where she can take a break. Libraries, museums, covered markets and cafés with comfortable chairs would all suit her well.

Fifth, no steep paths. Hills are the main thing to avoid. Even a gentle slope can be tiring for her on the way back, so please steer us away from anything that climbs steadily, unless there is a lift, a funicular or a road she can take instead.

To sum up, we are looking for short, flat, smooth routes with benches along the way, warm indoor places to rest, and no steep ground. I would be grateful if you could keep these in mind when suggesting activities, and tell me honestly if something on your list does not fit. We would rather know now than discover a problem halfway up a slope. Thank you for taking the time to understand what she needs.

Thoughts about the guesthouse room. We are staying in a small guesthouse for part of the trip, and I want to get the room right, since it will be our base for several nights. My mother will be sharing it with me, so comfort and convenience matter more than anything fancy.

The most important request is a ground floor room. Stairs are very hard for her, and even one flight can leave her exhausted or unsteady, so please make sure the room is on the ground level, with no steps between the entrance and the bed. If there is a step at the door, a ramp or a clear, well-lit route would help.

We would also love a sea view if one is available. My mother has always found the water calming, and waking up to the sea each morning would mean a great deal to her. A view is nice, but not at the cost of the ground floor request. If the only sea-facing room is upstairs, please let me know and we can talk it over.

A quiet corner is another priority. Rooms near the front desk, the kitchen or the street can be noisy, and she sleeps lightly. A room at the back, or one at the end of a corridor away from the lift and the entrance, would be ideal. If the guesthouse has a small sitting area or a bench in the garden, that would be a lovely place for her to rest in the afternoons.

Breakfast times are worth discussing as well. We are early risers, but we would prefer not to be rushed, and my mother likes to eat slowly. Could breakfast be served from around half past seven until nine or later? If the dining room has comfortable chairs and is not too crowded, even better. If there is a way for us to take a tray to the room on mornings when she is tired, that would be a kindness.

Finally, could you confirm whether the room has a private bathroom with a level entry and something to hold on to near the toilet? Many older rooms have high bathtubs, and a walk-in shower with a seat would make a real difference. If the bathroom is shared, please tell me so that we can plan accordingly.

Thank you for helping us find the right room. Please send me the options you have, including the floor, the view, the position in the building and the bathroom arrangements, so that I can compare them with my mother and make a choice that suits us both.

One last set of notes about the journey home. We are leaving on the final day of the trip, and I want the last morning to be as calm and unhurried as the rest of our time together. Here is what I have in mind, so that you can help us arrange it.

We will check out of the guesthouse around ten o'clock. Please confirm whether the guesthouse will hold our luggage for us after checkout, in case our train does not leave until the afternoon. A small storage room or a locked cupboard near the front desk would be perfect. If there is any charge, I would like to know it in advance.

Our luggage is two medium suitcases and a small bag for my mother's things, including her stick and folding seat. Please make sure any taxi or transfer we book can take all three without a squeeze, and that the driver is willing to help with the cases if needed. Level kerbs and a short walk from the car to the platform would suit her best.

Before we head to the station, we would like one last gentle walk. Something short and flat, no more than a kilometre, along the water or through a quiet square, with a bench where she can sit and look at the view one more time. I would be grateful if you could suggest a route that finishes near a café, so we can have a warm drink before the walk back.

Lunch comes next. We would like to eat somewhere indoors, with comfortable seating and no long queues, and close enough to the station that we do not need to rush. Ideally the restaurant serves soft food and simple dishes, and can seat us by a window if one is free. If you can reserve a table for a quarter past twelve, that would be wonderful.

Please also check the train times for us. We would like to leave the restaurant with at least forty minutes to spare before departure, so that my mother can walk to the platform without hurrying, and so that there is time to find a seat with a clear, level route from the entrance. If the station has a lift or a ramp, please let me know which platform it serves.

Thank you for helping us end the trip well. A calm departure means a great deal to my mother, and it means a lot to me too. Please send me a short plan for the final day when you have a moment, and we will confirm the details together.
